summary: Explains which documents make up the complete Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS), an abstract algorithm for applying dynamically retrieved string transformation rules to an application-unique string. Together with RFCs 3402 through 3404, it replaces RFCs 2168 and 2915 and updates RFC 2276.

eli5.summary: DDDS is a recipe for turning a name into a place to look it up, using rules fetched on the fly. This is the table of contents for the five documents that describe it.

questions: what is the dynamic delegation discovery system
subtitle: The roadmap that says which documents together make up the Dynamic Delegation Discovery System.

tldr.problem: The Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS) is split across several documents, and reading one without the others leads to misunderstandings and interoperability problems.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3401 lists the documents that make up the whole system: an algorithm, Applications that give it a concrete job, and Databases that store its rules.
tldr.outcome: Together with RFC 3402, RFC 3403 and RFC 3404 it obsoletes RFC 2168 and RFC 2915 and updates RFC 2276.

today: RFC 3401 is an Informational RFC that has not been obsoleted or updated. It replaced RFC 2168 and RFC 2915 together with RFCs 3402 to 3404, and it says readers should check the RFC repository for documents that update or obsolete it.

sections.title: What DDDS Is and Who Should Read This
sections.content:
The Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS) implements lazy binding of strings to data, in order to support dynamically configured delegation systems. It maps a unique string to data stored in a DDDS Database by repeatedly applying string transformation rules until a terminal condition is reached.

RFC 3401 is an Informational memo that defines the entire DDDS by listing the documents that make up the specification. It is meant for anyone implementing or trying to understand the generic DDDS algorithm, URI resolution, ENUM telephone number to URI resolution, and the NAPTR DNS resource record. The reader is warned that reading one document of the series without the others will probably lead to misunderstandings and interoperability problems.
sections.eli5: Imagine a treasure hunt where each clue tells you how to find the next clue until you reach the prize. DDDS is the rulebook for that kind of hunt, and this document tells you which booklets belong together.

sections.title: The Algorithm and Its Parts
sections.content:
The algorithm itself is defined by RFC 3402. That document defines the basic DDDS vocabulary, the algorithm, the requirements on applications using the algorithm, and the requirements on databases that store DDDS rules.

The algorithm alone is useless without a document that says how and why it is used. Those documents are called Applications, and they are not part of the DDDS core specification. Applications need places to keep their rules, called DDDS Databases, which are usually specified in separate documents that are also outside the core specification.
sections.eli5: The algorithm is like the rules of a board game. You still need a particular game to play and a box to keep the pieces in, and those come from other documents.

sections.title: Applications
sections.content:
No implementation can begin without an Application specification, because it supplies the concrete details for the algorithm. Without one, DDDS is nothing more than a general algorithm. An Application document defines four things:

  • the Application Unique String, the thing the delegation rules act on;
  • the First Well Known Rule, the rule that says where the process starts;
  • the list of valid Databases, since you cannot use just any Database;
  • the final expected output.

Two sample Applications are named. RFC 2916, "E.164 number and DNS", uses DDDS to map a telephone number to service endpoints such as SIP or email. RFC 3404 uses DDDS to resolve any URI to a set of endpoints or resolvers that can give more information about the URI, independent of its scheme.
sections.eli5: An Application says what you are looking for, where to begin, which boxes you may look in, and what the answer should look like. One example turns a phone number into a way to reach someone.

sections.title: Databases
sections.content:
Every DDDS Application must use some type of DDDS Database. A Database document defines how the Database works in general, the formats for Keys and for Rules, the Key lookup process, rule insertion procedures, and measures to avoid collisions.

A Database cannot be used on its own, and there must be at least one Application that uses it. Several Databases and Applications exist, and some Databases support more than one Application, but not every Application uses every Database. For that reason, compliance is defined by the combination of a Database specification and an Application specification.

The sample Database named is the DNS Database, which is also the official specification for the NAPTR DNS Resource Record. The memo's reference list identifies this as Part Three, RFC 3403.
sections.eli5: A Database is the filing cabinet where the rules are kept. It is only useful when some Application knows how to ask it questions.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
Known security issues that arise from using the algorithms and databases must be specified, completely and fully, in the respective specifications. The databases and algorithms are not required to be secure or risk free, but the known risks must be identified. Publishing a new database type or algorithm requires a security review, and the security considerations should keep being evaluated.

RFC 3401 creates no new requirements for the IANA itself, but the other documents in the series create many. The IANA is asked to review their IANA Considerations sections to find the full set of new registries and requirements.
sections.eli5: Anyone who adds a new piece must write down the dangers they know about, so users are not surprised later.
